objectives: Apply wildlife medicine + conservation principles (IUCN, WCS, sea turtles, raptors, deer).
Manage exotic-pet medicine (reptiles, parrots, small mammals).
Apply Russell-Burch 3Rs + the Guide for the Care and Use to laboratory-animal practice.

slides.title: Wildlife medicine: conservation, IUCN, + the work at the wild-domestic interface
slides.body:
**Wildlife medicine** sits at the intersection of veterinary medicine, ecology, conservation biology, + public health — and is one of the most rapidly expanding subdisciplines. The **American College of Zoological Medicine (ACZM)** + the **European College of Zoological Medicine (ECZM)** certify specialists; **AAZV** (American Association of Zoo Veterinarians) + **AAFV** (American Association of Wildlife Veterinarians) + **IUCN Wildlife Health Specialist Group** organize the global community.

**Conservation taxonomy + the IUCN Red List**:
- The **International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN)** maintains the global **Red List of Threatened Species** — categories from **Least Concern (LC)** to **Near Threatened (NT)**, **Vulnerable (VU)**, **Endangered (EN)**, **Critically Endangered (CR)**, **Extinct in the Wild (EW)**, **Extinct (EX)**. ~150,000+ species assessed.
- Veterinary work on threatened species is constrained by + integrated with IUCN, CITES (Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species, 1973), national endangered-species legislation (US Endangered Species Act 1973), + species-specific recovery plans.
- **Examples of veterinary-led recovery programs**: California condor (USFWS, San Diego + Los Angeles Zoo; lead-bullet poisoning is the dominant adult mortality), Yellowstone gray wolf reintroduction (USFWS + USGS NWHC), black-footed ferret (sylvatic plague + canine distemper management), Florida panther (genetic restoration, FIV, vehicular trauma), red wolf, whooping crane, Mexican wolf.

**Wildlife conservation organizations + the veterinary role**:
- **Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS)** — founded 1895; runs Bronx Zoo + multiple US zoos + ~500 field conservation projects globally; **William Karesh** led the WCS Field Veterinary Program for decades + co-articulated the **2004 Manhattan Principles**. WCS Health Program is one of the foundational One Health institutions.
- **IUCN Wildlife Health Specialist Group** + the global wildlife disease surveillance network.
- **USGS National Wildlife Health Center (NWHC)** — Madison, Wisconsin; US federal wildlife disease laboratory.
- **EcoHealth Alliance** (NYC, Peter Daszak) + WCS + Smithsonian Conservation Biology Institute + Tufts Conservation Medicine + Davis One Health Institute + many academic programs.
- **Field veterinary work**: capture + immobilization (Telazol/medetomidine/butorphanol or BAM; species + size + indication-specific dart-delivery + remote-injection systems), translocation, vaccination, contraception, disease surveillance, post-mortem investigation, reintroduction support.

**Major wildlife disease challenges**:
- **Sylvatic + zoonotic disease at the wildlife-livestock interface**: brucellosis in bison + elk; chronic wasting disease (CWD) in deer + elk + moose — a prion disease spreading across North America + into Europe + Korea; tuberculosis (M. bovis) in white-tailed deer (Michigan), badgers (UK), African buffalo; African swine fever in wild boar (Europe + Asia); HPAI in wild birds + marine mammals.
- **Lead poisoning** in raptors + waterfowl + scavengers (eagles, vultures, condors) from spent lead ammunition + fishing tackle; severe + chronic; advocacy for nontoxic alternatives.
- **Anthropogenic trauma**: vehicular, electrocution (raptors on power lines), wind turbines, building strikes (passerines), entanglement (cetaceans, sea turtles), oil spills, plastic ingestion (seabirds + sea turtles).
- **Climate-driven**: range shifts of vectors (Lyme moving north, white-nose syndrome in bats — *Pseudogymnoascus destructans* — decimating eastern North American bat populations); coral disease; coral bleaching; pinniped + cetacean disease outbreaks.
- **Wildlife trade + emerging disease**: bushmeat, exotic-pet trade, traditional medicine — all major drivers of biodiversity loss + zoonotic spillover.

**Specific clinical wildlife groups**:
- **Deer (white-tailed, mule, elk, moose)**: CWD (top priority), hemorrhagic disease (EHD, BTV — culicoid-vectored), parasitism, vehicular trauma, lead exposure. CWD is a TSE (transmissible spongiform encephalopathy) prion disease + the leading wildlife-disease crisis in North America.
- **Raptors (eagles, hawks, owls, falcons)**: lead poisoning (#1 chronic threat), rodenticide secondary toxicosis (anticoagulant rodenticides — brodifacoum, bromadiolone), trichomoniasis (Trichomonas gallinae — 'frounce' in raptors), aspergillosis, West Nile, electrocution, vehicular trauma. Veterinary care at raptor centers (Raptor Center at U of Minnesota — Patrick Redig; National Eagle Center; many wildlife rehabilitators).
- **Sea turtles (loggerhead, green, leatherback, Kemp's ridley, hawksbill, olive ridley)**: cold-stunning (mass strandings, esp. New England), fibropapillomatosis (herpesvirus + likely cofactors), entanglement, plastic ingestion, vessel strike, dredging. **All sea turtle species** are listed under IUCN + ESA — work coordinated with NOAA, USFWS, + sea-turtle stranding networks. Veterinary care: rehydration, antibiotics, surgical FB removal, fibropapilloma resection, prolonged rehabilitation, eventual release with tag/transmitter.
- **Marine mammals (cetaceans + pinnipeds)**: mass strandings, morbillivirus outbreaks, harmful algal bloom toxicosis (domoic acid in sea lions; brevetoxin in dolphins + manatees), entanglement, vessel strike. NOAA Marine Mammal Health + Stranding Response Program + The Marine Mammal Center (Sausalito, CA).
- **Bats**: white-nose syndrome (devastating eastern NA bat populations 2007+), rabies surveillance, lyssaviruses, Nipah/Hendra/SARS-related coronavirus reservoirs — vital from One Health perspective.

slides.title: Zoo medicine + exotic pets: reptiles, parrots, small mammals
slides.body:
**Zoo medicine** is the formal subspecialty of captive-wild-animal practice. Modern accredited zoos (AZA — Association of Zoos + Aquariums; EAZA in Europe) have **species survival plans (SSPs)**, full-time veterinary teams, specialty diagnostic capability, + research programs. Zoo + wildlife + exotic-pet medicine share much; the books — *Fowler's Zoo + Wild Animal Medicine* (multi-volume), *Mader's Reptile + Amphibian Medicine + Surgery* (3rd ed. 2019), *Quesenberry + Carpenter's Ferrets, Rabbits + Rodents* (4th ed. 2020), *Speer's Current Therapy in Avian Medicine + Surgery* — are foundational.

**Exotic-pet practice** has grown into a major sector — millions of US households keep reptiles, birds, ferrets, rabbits, guinea pigs, hamsters, gerbils, hedgehogs, sugar gliders, chinchillas, prairie dogs (limited), small primates (mostly illegal), invertebrates.

**Reptile medicine** (extending the lesson-2 anatomy + thermoregulation framework):
- **Metabolic bone disease (nutritional secondary hyperparathyroidism)** — most common pet-reptile illness; UVB + Ca + D₃ + temperature husbandry failure; rubber jaw + pathologic fractures + paresis + anorexia. Treat with calcium + calcitriol + corrected husbandry.
- **Husbandry-related disease** dominates: incorrect POTZ (preferred optimum temperature zone), inadequate UVB exposure (most pet-store fluorescents inadequate; T5 high-output Arcadia/Zoo Med + Solarmeter measurement is the modern standard), inappropriate humidity, dystocia from poor nesting opportunity, substrate impaction.
- **Infectious**: Salmonella (zoonotic + nearly universal), inclusion body disease (boas + pythons; reptarenavirus), cryptosporidiosis (snakes; usually fatal), mycobacteriosis, ranavirus + chytrid fungus (Bd, Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis — devastating to amphibians globally).
- **Anesthesia**: alfaxalone or propofol IV (jugular, ventral coccygeal vein) + isoflurane maintenance; long induction + recovery; minute ventilation low; intubate + IPPV; recover at appropriate temperature (~30 °C).
- **Surgery**: ovariosalpingectomy in egg-bound reptiles, mass removal, prolapse repair, abscess debridement (reptile pus is caseous + must be excised, not drained).
- **Anatomical landmark**: renal portal system means caudal-half injections can pass through kidney first — drug dosing implications.

**Avian medicine (parrots primarily)**:
- **Psittacine beak + feather disease (PBFD)** — circovirus; immunosuppression + feather + beak dystrophy; common in cockatoos + lovebirds + budgerigars; no treatment.
- **Polyomavirus** in young psittacines.
- **Avian Bornavirus + Proventricular Dilation Disease (PDD)**: weight loss + regurgitation + GI motility disorder.
- **Aspergillosis** (Aspergillus fumigatus) — fungal pneumonia + air sacculitis; chronic + difficult to treat (itraconazole, voriconazole, amphotericin B nebulization).
- **Heavy-metal toxicosis** — lead + zinc; common in caged birds chewing cage metal, fishing weights, foil; treat with chelation (calcium-EDTA, succimer).
- **Self-mutilation + feather-destructive behavior**: complex psychogenic + medical; differential includes giardiasis, mites, dermatophytosis, allergic, hormonal, social, environmental.
- **Egg binding (dystocia) + reproductive disease**: hen on calcium + proper diet + uncoupled from mirror/perch/owner-as-mate; chronic egg laying common in cockatoos.
- **Anesthesia**: mask induction with isoflurane is straightforward; intubate (uncuffed; complete tracheal rings risk pressure necrosis); air-sac flush common for surgical access.

**Small mammal exotics**:
- **Rabbits**: gastric stasis (#1 emergency — pain → ileus → bacterial overgrowth → death; treat aggressively with fluids, motility agents [metoclopramide, cisapride], analgesia, force-feeding Critical Care, +/- antibiotics if E. cuniculi or pasteurellosis); dental disease (hypselodont cheek teeth + malocclusion); pasteurellosis (Pasteurella multocida — 'snuffles'); encephalitozoonosis (E. cuniculi — head tilt + cataracts + paresis); uterine adenocarcinoma (~80% of unspayed >5-yr-old rabbits — strongly advocate OHE); RHDV2 (rabbit hemorrhagic disease virus 2 — recent US emergence, deadly).
- **Ferrets**: insulinoma (hypoglycemia + seizures + collapse — surgical + medical management with diazoxide + steroids); adrenal disease (hyperadrenocorticism: alopecia + vulvar enlargement + pruritus + behavioral — deslorelin SC implant or surgical adrenalectomy); lymphoma; gastric Helicobacter; canine distemper (vaccine essential, fatal otherwise); influenza (humans → ferrets bidirectional zoonosis).
- **Guinea pigs**: hypovitaminosis C (cannot synthesize vit C — dietary requirement); dental malocclusion; ovarian cysts; pneumonia (Bordetella + Streptococcus).
- **Hamsters + gerbils + mice + rats**: short lifespans; spontaneous neoplasia (mammary in rats); respiratory mycoplasmosis (rats); proliferative ileitis (hamsters); diabetes (Mongolian gerbils).
- **Hedgehogs**: wobbly hedgehog syndrome (demyelinating); neoplasia rates very high; mites + dermatophytosis.

**Zoonotic risk** in exotic-pet practice is substantial — Salmonella (reptiles + amphibians, esp. for children/immunocompromised), psittacosis (birds → atypical pneumonia humans), mycobacteriosis, monkeypox (exotic rodents → 2003 US outbreak), avian influenza, herpes B (primates — fatal in humans, primate-pet ownership ethically + medically discouraged). Veterinarians counsel responsibly + report appropriately.

slides.title: Laboratory animal medicine: Russell-Burch 3Rs, AALAS, + the Guide
slides.body:
**Laboratory animal medicine** is the formal subspecialty supporting biomedical research with animal models. The **American College of Laboratory Animal Medicine (ACLAM)** certifies specialists; **ACVMA**, **AVMA**, **AALAS** organize the field.

**The 3Rs — Russell + Burch (1959)**:
**William Russell + Rex Burch** wrote *The Principles of Humane Experimental Technique* (1959) — the foundational ethical + scientific framework for animal research. Their **3Rs** principles structure all modern research-animal use globally:
1. **Replacement** — replace animal use with non-animal alternatives wherever possible: in vitro cell culture, organoids + organ-on-chip, computational models, in silico simulation, imaging studies in humans, lower phyla where defensible (invertebrates, microbes).
2. **Reduction** — minimize the number of animals used through statistical experimental design (power analysis, factorial designs, pre-registration, ARRIVE 2.0 reporting guidelines), data sharing, meta-analytic synthesis.
3. **Refinement** — minimize suffering + improve welfare for animals that ARE used: environmental enrichment (NRC + NIH guidance), pair/group housing, gentle handling (Hurst + West 2010 tunnel handling for mice), positive reinforcement training, refined anesthesia + analgesia, humane endpoints, attention to species-specific behavior + needs.

The 3Rs are now universally adopted: NIH, NSF, FDA, EU Directive 2010/63/EU, AAALAC accreditation, USDA Animal Welfare Act, the UK ASPA, + every funder + regulator.

**The Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals (8th edition, 2011)**: NRC/ILAR — the bedrock US regulatory + best-practice document. Topics: institutional structure (IACUC — Institutional Animal Care + Use Committee), veterinary care, husbandry, occupational health + safety, physical plant + environmental conditions, species-specific standards. Required compliance for any institution receiving NIH/PHS funding.

**Regulatory architecture (US)**:
- **Animal Welfare Act (AWA, 1966)** + USDA APHIS Animal Care enforcement; covers most species in research, exhibition, breeding, dealers — but **excludes mice + rats of the genus Mus + Rattus bred for research, birds, livestock used in agricultural research, + cold-blooded species**. (~95% of research animals are excluded mice/rats — covered instead by PHS Policy + the Guide.)
- **PHS Policy on Humane Care + Use of Laboratory Animals** (NIH OLAW) — covers ALL vertebrate animal use in PHS-funded research.
- **IACUC** — institutional committee of veterinarians, scientists, ethicists, community members reviewing every animal-use protocol; mandatory continuing approval.
- **AAALAC International** (Association for Assessment + Accreditation of Laboratory Animal Care) — voluntary peer-reviewed accreditation; most major US + many international institutions accredited.
- **AALAS (American Association for Laboratory Animal Science)** — professional society + training + certification (LAT, LATG, AALAS technicians + veterinarians).

**Major species in biomedical research + the veterinary subspecialty's scope**:
- **Mice + rats** (~95% of research animals): genetic models (knockout, transgenic, conditional, humanized; CRISPR-engineered), behavioral, cancer, immunology, neuroscience, drug discovery, toxicology. **Charles River, Jackson Laboratory, Taconic, Envigo** are major commercial suppliers + strain repositories. Mouse genetics (Jackson, Wellcome) underlies most modern biomedicine.
- **Zebrafish (Danio rerio)**: vertebrate genetic model — embryonic development, drug screening, regeneration, neuroscience, cardiovascular.
- **Rabbits**: antibody production, atherosclerosis, ophthalmology, surgical training.
- **Pigs**: large-animal preclinical models — cardiovascular, transplantation (xenotransplantation, eg recent UAB + Mass General pig-kidney + pig-heart transplants), surgical training.
- **Non-human primates (rhesus + cynomolgus macaques + marmosets + others)**: rare + tightly regulated; preclinical for vaccines (HIV, SIV, COVID-19), neuroscience, infectious disease. **The 2014+ NIH halt of chimpanzee research** + sanctuary placement reflected ethical evolution; macaque + marmoset use remains.
- **Cats + dogs**: limited, regulated; some pharmacology, cardiology, orthopedic research; companion-animal clinical trials use client-owned animals with informed consent (Veterinary Cancer Society + COTC — Comparative Oncology Trials Consortium — at NCI).
- **Agricultural research**: cattle + sheep + swine + chickens in nutrition + reproduction + production research; AWA-exempt but covered by ARRP + AAALAC + university policies.

**Lab animal veterinarian roles**:
- Direct veterinary care + medicine + surgery for research animals.
- IACUC engagement + protocol review + 3Rs implementation.
- Anesthesia + analgesia consultation for invasive studies.
- Health surveillance (sentinel + PCR + serology for excluded pathogens — Helicobacter, MNV, MPV, MHV, mouse parvovirus, Sendai, ectromelia, etc.).
- Occupational health + biosafety (BSL-2, BSL-3, ABSL-3 + 4 for infectious work).
- Disaster + emergency planning.
- Training of research staff in handling + technique.
- Comparative-medicine consultation — selecting species + model, designing controls, reading the relevant clinical + spontaneous-disease literature.

**Comparative medicine** — the discipline tying everything together: spontaneous animal disease informs human medicine + vice versa. Dog comparative oncology (osteosarcoma, lymphoma, mammary, bladder TCC — COTC, NCI, Morris Animal Foundation, AKC Canine Health Foundation, V Foundation) has shaped human oncology. Cat HCM, dog DCM, equine PPID, sheep prion (scrapie), bovine BSE — Schwabe's 'one medicine' (1964) operationalized at the bench. Russell + Burch + the Guide + IACUC + AAALAC + ACLAM form the ethical + regulatory infrastructure that lets the comparative-medicine engine run.

question.question: Design + execute a sea-turtle cold-stun rescue + rehabilitation protocol
question.goal: Apply wildlife + zoo + rehabilitation medicine to an actual mass-stranding scenario.

steps.prompt: Cold-stunning: what is the pathophysiology + which sea-turtle species + regions are affected?

acceptedAnswers: ectotherm hypothermia from sudden water-temperature drop; Kemp's ridley, loggerhead, green; mainly Cape Cod Bay + similar northeast US locations + UK + EU

steps.reveal: **Sea turtles are ectotherms**; when water temperature drops below ~10 °C their metabolism + locomotion shut down, they cannot move to deeper warm water + are pushed onto beaches by tides. Common in **Cape Cod Bay, Massachusetts** (Kemp's ridleys + loggerheads + greens — IUCN Critically Endangered Kemp's ridley is the highest-profile species), also UK + EU coasts in cold years. Annual mass strandings of dozens-to-hundreds; New England Aquarium + Mass Audubon + NOAA + USFWS coordinate response.

steps.prompt: Field response + transport: what is the protocol on the beach?

acceptedAnswers: do not rush to warm; gradual rewarming over 24-48 h; transport in dry insulated tote; do not place in water; document + ID + measure
gradual warming over days — sudden warming kills

steps.reveal: **Critical principle**: **sudden rewarming kills**. Cold-stunned turtles must be warmed gradually over ~24-48 h, ~5 °C per day. Place in dry, insulated tote at slightly-above-ambient temperature; do NOT immerse in water (may drown — buoyancy + breathing-reflex compromised). Document: species, size, location, condition; tag if not previously tagged; transport to coordinated rehab facility (New England Aquarium, NMLC — National Marine Life Center, NC Aquariums for southern strandings). Coordinate with NOAA + USFWS as ESA-listed species.

acceptedAnswers: physical exam, blood work, radiographs, gradual warming, fluids, supportive nutrition, antibiotics if pneumonia, antifungals if mycotic, weeks-to-months rehabilitation
blood gas + chem + CBC + radiographs + slow rewarming + fluids + nutrition + antibiotics for pneumonia + months of rehab

steps.reveal: **Workup**: physical (BCS, hydration, alertness, neuro), blood gas + chem + CBC (acidosis + electrolyte derangement + leukocytosis common), radiographs (pneumonia is the #1 secondary complication — fungal + bacterial in cold-stressed turtles). **Treatment**: gradual rewarming (5 °C/day from ~8 °C to ~24 °C over a week or two); IV/SC fluids (saline + LRS); enteral nutrition once awake + interested (squid, fish, special turtle gel diets); antibiotics for pneumonia (ceftazidime, enrofloxacin); antifungals (voriconazole, terbinafine) for fungal pneumonia; physical therapy + swimming sessions; weeks-to-months rehabilitation.

acceptedAnswers: release to warm waters (southern US in winter); satellite-tag transmitters; coordinate with NOAA + ESA; long-term tracking
release to appropriate warm-water zone (Florida or Gulf), satellite tag, NOAA coordination

steps.reveal: **Release** to appropriate warm-water habitat (Gulf of Mexico, southern Atlantic, Florida) — often via plane transport in winter; coordinate with NOAA + USFWS; satellite-tag a subset (Argos PTT or Fastloc-GPS — Wildlife Computers, Lotek) for post-release tracking + habitat-use research. Survival data from rehabilitation programs (~60-80% successful release; reasonable post-release survival for monitored cohorts) supports the conservation investment. **The cold-stun rehabilitation pipeline** illustrates how wildlife veterinary medicine integrates triage + clinical care + conservation biology + multi-agency coordination + research — a model for endangered-species recovery generally.

question.question: Why are the Russell-Burch 3Rs (Replacement, Reduction, Refinement) considered the foundational ethical + scientific framework for animal research?
options: Russell + Burch's *The Principles of Humane Experimental Technique* (1959) introduced the **3Rs — Replacement, Reduction, Refinement** — as a unified framework for ethical + scientific improvement of animal research. **Replacement**: use non-animal alternatives where possible (cell culture, organoids, organ-on-chip, in silico models, human imaging studies, lower phyla). **Reduction**: minimize animal numbers via statistical experimental design (power analysis, factorial designs, pre-registration, ARRIVE 2.0 reporting), data sharing, meta-analysis. **Refinement**: improve welfare for animals used — environmental enrichment, pair/group housing, gentle handling (Hurst + West 2010 mouse tunnel handling), positive-reinforcement training, refined anesthesia + analgesia, humane endpoints, species-appropriate behavior. The framework is **simultaneously ethical (reduces suffering), scientific (improves data quality — stressed animals produce noisy + non-reproducible data), + practical (organizes regulation + funding + institutional review)**. It is universally adopted: NIH, NSF, FDA, EU Directive 2010/63/EU, AAALAC, USDA AWA, UK ASPA + the *Guide for the Care + Use of Laboratory Animals* (8th ed. 2011) operationalize the 3Rs throughout. ACLAM + AALAS train + certify the professionals who implement them. Sixty-five years on, the 3Rs remain the single most important framework in research-animal welfare — a 1959 ethics + design innovation that scaled to a global regulatory architecture.
question.explanation: Russell-Burch 1959 3Rs (Replacement, Reduction, Refinement) are the universal framework — ethical (reduces suffering) + scientific (improves data quality) + practical (regulatory architecture). Adopted by NIH, EU, FDA, AAALAC, USDA AWA + the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals (8th ed.) globally.

slides.workedSolution: Russell + Burch (1959) 3Rs: Replacement (non-animal alternatives), Reduction (statistical design + ARRIVE), Refinement (welfare). Universal regulatory + ethical framework — NIH/NSF/FDA/AAALAC/USDA AWA/EU/UK + the Guide for the Care + Use of Lab Animals 8e operationalize. Both ethical + scientifically rigorous (stressed animals produce noisy data). ACLAM + AALAS train professionals to implement.

question.question: A juvenile bald eagle is presented to a wildlife rehab center, ataxic + weak + with green-stained feathers around the cloaca. Apply wildlife medicine reasoning + the conservation framework.
question.scenario: Diagnose + manage lead toxicosis in a raptor, with conservation context.
question.modelAnswer: **Top differential**: **lead toxicosis** — the most common chronic threat to scavenging raptors (eagles, vultures, condors). Bald eagles scavenge gut piles + carcasses of hunted deer + waterfowl + ingest lead fragments from spent lead ammunition (small fragments scatter from rifle bullets + shotgun shells); chronic + acute lead poisoning is widespread + devastating. **Clinical signs**: weakness + ataxia + 'mews' droop (drooping wings + carpal joint extension), bright green-stained feces (biliverdin staining from hepatic injury), seizures, blindness, anemia, regurgitation, eventually death. Lead also depresses immunity + may secondarily allow aspergillosis + other infections. **Workup**: (1) gentle restraint + thorough physical (BCS, hydration, neuro, ophthalmic); (2) **blood lead level** (point-of-care LeadCare II analyzer is standard at raptor centers — Patrick Redig + University of Minnesota Raptor Center pioneered protocols; >2 µg/dL is abnormal, >6 µg/dL clinical, >60 µg/dL severe + life-threatening); (3) **radiographs of GI tract + skull** (visible lead fragments? embedded shot? skull fracture from collision?); (4) CBC (regenerative anemia + basophilic stippling), chemistry (hepatic + renal), PCV/TS; (5) screen for concurrent disease (West Nile, trichomoniasis, aspergillosis, secondary anticoagulant rodenticide). **Treatment**: (1) **chelation** — **calcium-EDTA** (Ca-EDTA) 35 mg/kg SC q12h × 5 d, or **succimer (DMSA)** oral 30 mg/kg PO q12h × 14 d, or combinations; recheck blood lead + repeat cycles as needed. (2) **GI lead-fragment removal** if present — endoscopic retrieval (in larger fragments), surgical, or 'wash-out' via peanut-oil lavage. (3) **Supportive care**: fluids, nutritional support (whole-prey diet or carnivore-formula tube feeding), seizure control (diazepam, levetiracetam), antibiotics if secondary infection, ophthalmic care if blindness. (4) **Flight + behavioral conditioning** during weeks-to-months rehabilitation; pre-release flight tests (creance line + free flight); only release birds restored to physiological + functional normal. **Conservation context**: bald eagle is **delisted from US ESA** (recovery 2007) but still federally protected under Bald + Golden Eagle Protection Act + Migratory Bird Treaty Act; **lead poisoning is the #1 chronic mortality factor in eagles + condors + scavenger raptors**. **Advocacy** + policy work (USFWS lead-ammo ban on federal lands in waterfowl hunting since 1991; California ban 2019; voluntary conversion to copper bullets, NPS lead-ammo bans, Peregrine Fund + Audubon work) is part of the wildlife veterinarian's role — Schwabe-style One Health applied to the lead-ammunition pathway. **Post-release tracking** (Argos PTT, GPS, GSM) by partners (Raptor Center MN, HawkWatch International, USGS) generates the data that demonstrates lead's population impact + drives the policy case. **Outcome**: ~30-60% of lead-poisoned eagles presented for treatment can be successfully rehabilitated + released; severe cases + those with neurological deficits often cannot. Each released bird is both clinical success + conservation contribution.
question.rubric: Identifies lead toxicosis in raptor (top differential + signs), measures blood lead, uses Ca-EDTA + supportive care, removes GI fragments, addresses conservation + policy context (lead-ammo + USFWS + state bans + Peregrine Fund + Raptor Center), references rehabilitation + release + post-release tracking, demonstrates wildlife medicine as integrating clinical care + conservation biology + policy.

question.question: A research lab plans a mouse behavioral study comparing 4 genotypes × 2 sexes × 2 ages = 16 groups. Power analysis indicates n=8 per group is needed. Calculate total mice. Apply the 3Rs.
acceptedAnswers: 16 × 8 = 128 mice; Reduction: justify with power analysis (already done) + consider factorial design reducing further; Replacement: in silico/in vitro pre-screening; Refinement: enrichment + group housing + handling protocols

128 mice total; apply 3Rs — Reduction (power analysis justifies n; consider sequential design); Replacement (in vitro/in silico precursors); Refinement (enrichment + tunnel handling + analgesia + humane endpoints)
question.explanation: **Math**: 4 × 2 × 2 × 8 = **128 mice**. **3Rs application**: (1) **Replacement** — were in vitro / in silico / behavioral assays in lower phyla considered? Could the question be addressed with fewer groups? Could a published dataset answer part of the question? (2) **Reduction** — n = 8/group is reasonable for behavioral assays with moderate effect size; factorial design used appropriately captures interactions efficiently (much better than testing each factor separately); consider sequential / adaptive design that allows stopping early if signal is clear; pre-register protocol + use ARRIVE 2.0 reporting. (3) **Refinement** — enrichment per Guide; same-sex group housing; **gentle handling (Hurst + West 2010 tunnel handling** — picking mice up by tail elevates stress hormones + behavior outcomes; cupped-hand + tunnel handling improves welfare + reduces variability); operant chamber design avoiding aversive stimuli where possible; humane endpoints + analgesia for any invasive procedures; appropriate light/dark cycle + acclimatization. **IACUC review** mandatory + considers all of the above. The math is the easy part; the 3Rs application is the discipline.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain why the Russell-Burch 3Rs + the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals (8e) + the IUCN/CITES wildlife framework form the ethical infrastructure of comparative-animal medicine across the three pillars (wildlife, exotic, laboratory).
question.rubric: Mentions: (1) Russell + Burch (1959) 3Rs — Replacement, Reduction, Refinement — universal research-animal welfare framework; (2) the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals (NRC/ILAR 8th ed. 2011) + IACUC + AAALAC + USDA AWA + PHS Policy operationalize the 3Rs; (3) IUCN Red List + CITES + ESA + national wildlife laws structure wildlife veterinary work + the role of WCS + Karesh + the Manhattan Principles + IUCN Wildlife Health Specialist Group; (4) ACLAM + AALAS + ACZM + AAZV + ECZM + AAFV + ECVAA train the professionals; (5) the three pillars (wildlife, exotic, laboratory) share comparative-medicine principles + zoonosis surveillance + One Health framing — wildlife veterinary work informs both ecology + public health, exotic-pet practice generates zoonotic-disease intelligence, laboratory medicine drives biomedical research. Concludes that the ethical + regulatory infrastructure is what allows comparative animal medicine to function as a humane + scientifically valuable discipline.
